cases.title: Explosion at the BGRIMM explosives plant, Chambishi
cases.point: Centroid of the Chambishi Mine industrial area (OpenStreetMap way 251021938, tagged landuse=industrial, industrial=mine). The explosives plant stood on the grounds of the Chambishi copper mine. VOA put the mine about 350 km north of Lusaka; the Mail & Guardian put it about 300 km north of Lusaka.

lenders.name: BGRIMM (Chinese state-owned) and NFC Africa Mining Plc, owners of the plant
lenders.role: No lender financed the plant. The link to the Chinese state is ownership. Dow Jones Newswires reported on 12 October 2005 that BGRIMM (600980.SH), a Chinese government-owned company, held 60% of BGRIMM Zambia and that NFC Africa Plc owned the rest, NFC Africa itself being controlled by the Chinese government's China Non Ferrous Metal Industries (000758.SZ) with the Zambian government holding a minority stake.

lenders.name: Government of China (cash grant after the blast)
lenders.role: AidData record 2234: a $500,000 cash grant with food and blankets, given to the Government of Zambia in 2005 after the fatal accident at the CNMC-owned BGRIMM explosives plant. AidData's record places the plant in the town of Kitwe and its location note places it on the grounds of the Chambishi mine. The money followed the explosion; it did not finance the plant, and it is not the basis of this entry. No World Bank P-number exists for this financing.

cases.conditions: No lender financed the plant. The Chinese money AidData records against this event is the $500,000 relief grant that followed the explosion (AidData record 2234); the tie to the Chinese state is the state ownership of the companies that owned and ran the plant.

companies.name: BGRIMM Zambia (BGRIMM explosives plant)
companies.role: Owner and operator of the explosives plant that blew up
companies.desc: Explosives maker at Chambishi, 60% held by the Chinese government-owned company BGRIMM, listed in Shanghai as 600980.SH; NFC Africa Plc owns the rest (Dow Jones Newswires, 12 October 2005).

companies.name: NFC Africa Mining Plc
companies.role: Minority owner of the plant and operator of the Chambishi copper mine on whose grounds it stood
companies.desc: Copper producer at Chambishi controlled by the Chinese state group China Non Ferrous Metal Industries, listed as 000758.SZ, with the Zambian government holding a minority stake; nearly 2,000 miners worked at the site when Dow Jones Newswires visited in October 2005.

cases.community: The explosives plant blew up mid-morning on a Wednesday in April 2005. A day later police put the toll at at least 51 and said it might rise because many miners at the plant were still missing; government investigators said it was still not clear how many people had been working at the factory, and that they did not yet know what caused the blast (VOA, drawing on AFP, AP and Reuters). Zambia's mines minister, Kaunda Lembalemba, said the toll was believed to be over 50 and that the government and the plant's owners were at odds over the number of dead. He gave the owners 24 hours to produce a list of all their workers, dead or alive, and said: "I am very upset with them. They can't be treating human beings like pigs." He said the plant's management had not kept records of the casual workers it hired by the day, so the government asked Zambians with missing relatives to come forward. Lembalemba said two workers who survived had been admitted to the Chinese-run Sino-Zam hospital in the Copperbelt in stable condition. A survivor, Andrew Chewe, said: "It seems there was laxity on the part of management in terms of ensuring the safety of workers. We need an enquiry." Relatives waited outside the plant gate to identify the bodies (Mail & Guardian, 21 April 2005). In October 2005 Dow Jones Newswires reported that the graves of 49 workers killed in the April accident lay near the mine entrance, marked with white name labels and flowers. One of the 49 was Petronelar Namuntenda, 25. Her father, Clementine Mwangalala, who heard the explosion from his farm three kilometres away, said the company had promised compensation and it had not come: "They gave some money to help with the funeral. After that we haven't been given the compensation." The mines minister by then, Kalombo Mwansa, said "the question of compensation is still ongoing". The same report put deaths in Zambian mining accidents at at least 71 so far that year, on the Mineworkers Union of Zambia's count, against Chamber of Mines counts of 14 in 2004, 11 in 2003 and 14 in 2002. Xu Ruiyong, a manager at NFC Africa with an office at the mine complex, said there was no link between mining accidents in China and this one, declined to take the reporter to the site of the explosion, and said work at the plant "stopped completely" after the blast; he put the safety record at the Chambishi mine at "if not the best, I would say almost the best", and said there had been one fatality at the mine that year (Dow Jones Newswires, 12 October 2005). AidData's record adds that two people were injured.
cases.killed_note: killed holds 49, the only figure in these reports given as a count rather than a floor: Dow Jones Newswires, six months after the blast, describes "the graves of 49 workers killed in April" at the mine entrance and names one of them (12 October 2005). The earlier figures are floors: police put the toll at "at least 51" the day after and said it might rise because many workers were still missing (VOA); the mines minister said it was "believed to be over 50" and that the government and the owners were at odds over the number (Mail & Guardian, 21 April 2005). AidData's record states a flat 51 killed and 2 injured. The owners never produced the worker list the minister demanded and the minister said the plant kept no records of its casual workers, so no source establishes how many people were on shift.
cases.outcome: President Levy Mwanawasa said he was extremely grieved at the loss of life and ordered the mines minister to open an immediate investigation (Mail & Guardian, 21 April 2005). VOA reported the day after the blast that investigators did not yet know what had caused it. In October 2005 Dow Jones Newswires reported that the accidents had prompted government investigations into the explosion and into safety across the industry; that the mines minister, Kalombo Mwansa, declined to comment on the cause with the investigation under way; that a mining ministry official said witnesses had said the company ignored safety measures and produced two dangerous chemicals at the same time; and that workers blamed the rise in deaths mainly on the use of contract workers with less training than permanent staff. No published finding of the government investigation was located.

The Mail & Guardian reported in April 2005 that copper mining generated about 60% of Zambia's foreign earnings and that Chinese and Indian investors had moved in over the preceding years to buy major stakes in the mines.

cases.title: Neshe dam: compensation not paid as promised and abandoned resettlement houses
cases.place: Neshe (Amerti Neshi) dam, East Wollega Zone, Oromia Regional State, Ethiopia
cases.point: Amerti Neshi power plant, tagged 95 MW hydro (OpenStreetMap way 845221791). The dam and the resettlement area lie nearby, on the Neshi River at the edge of the escarpment.

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: One subsidiary buyer's credit loan for the Neshe dam, signed on 20 September 2007 by China Eximbank and the state-owned Commercial Bank of Ethiopia under a $500 million buyer's credit facility agreement of November 2006 between China Eximbank and Ethiopia's Ministry of Finance and Economic Development. The loan was worth about $125.205 million (ETB 1,082,214,356) and was provided in two tranches for two lots: 53.7% of its face value, $71,742,465 (ETB 581,478,798), for the civil works contract (AidData record 92137), and 46.3%, $57,969,915 (ETB 500,735,558), for the electro-mechanical contract (AidData record 92164). All subsidiary loans under the facility carried a 13-year maturity and interest of LIBOR plus a 2-3% margin and were secured against Ethiopia's export receipts to China, with those receipts overseen by the Commercial Bank of Ethiopia; AidData estimates the all-in rate itself, by adding the midpoint of that margin to the September 2007 six-month LIBOR. The money was to cover about 85% of a $147.3 million (ETB 1.3 billion) contract between the Ethiopian Electric Power Corporation and China Gezhouba Group Corporation signed in December 2006. Ethiopia's Aid Management Platform records the civil works tranche 58% disbursed, ETB 336,241,047 in 7 disbursements between 2010 and 2012, and the electro-mechanical tranche 104% disbursed, ETB 521,882,224 in 8 disbursements between 2009 and 2012 (AidData records 92137 and 92164). A field study of the scheme gives the cost differently, as 85% of construction costs of US$137 million (Mueller-Mahn and Gebreyes, Land 8(9):135, 5 September 2019). No World Bank P-number exists for this financing.

cases.conditions: Loans under the 2006 facility were collateralised against Ethiopia's export receipts to China, which at the time were mainly sesame seed receipts, and the facility required that all Ethiopian export receipts to China be overseen by the Commercial Bank of Ethiopia. The loan proceeds were tied to the contract with China Gezhouba Group Corporation (AidData records 45047, 92137 and 92164).

companies.name: China Gezhouba Group Corporation (CGGC)
companies.role: General EPC contractor for the dam, under a contract signed in December 2006

companies.name: Ethiopian Electric Power Corporation (EEPCo)
companies.role: State power utility that signed the construction contract and built the scheme
companies.desc: Ethiopian state-owned enterprise that generates and transmits the country's electricity; it operates the Amerti Neshi plant, which OpenStreetMap records under its short name EEPCO as the plant's operator.

companies.name: Fincha Sugar Factory (Finchaa Sugar Estate)
companies.role: State-owned sugar estate next to the dam; its managers planted the out-growers' land with sugar cane in 2017 and stopped paying rent for it in the second year
companies.desc: State-owned sugar factory and plantation in the lower Fincha valley. The plantation that the scheme irrigates grew from 6,000 to almost 20,000 hectares as the state farm was converted from grain to sugar cane (Land 8(9):135).

cases.community: The dam was built on the Neshi River, as AidData spells it, or the Neshe River, as the field study spells it, with construction starting on 22 July 2010. It was the third stage of the Fincha-Amerti-Neshe scheme, and it fed a sugar cane plantation that grew from 6,000 to almost 20,000 hectares. A field study by Detlef Mueller-Mahn and Million Gebreyes of the University of Bonn, published on 5 September 2019, says exact resettlement figures are difficult to find and that, according to the people interviewed for the study, the number of households resettled for the Neshe dam was approximately 1,200. People told the researchers that only village administrators and people close to them were told of the plans, that there was no consultation with the whole community, and that they were promised houses with showers and electricity, ten years of subsistence allowances and two hybrid cows a household. The study reports: "Many respondents confirmed that compensation for land that was taken for the new dam was not paid as originally agreed, which, as they explain, was due to insufficient asset valuations, incorrect surveys, mismanagement, and corruption." Families who were resettled found the new houses in the lowland near the plantation were not as nice as they had expected and that living conditions there were not favourable, so many left the new settlement, went back to the highlands and abandoned the houses and the land they had been given. As out-growers they were no longer free to decide what to grow or where to live, but had to grow sugar cane for the factory. In 2017 the plantation's farm managers found the out-growers' land no longer cultivated and started to plant it with sugar cane. The settlers said the sugar company should pay them rent; it did so in the first year, refused in the second, and people threatened to burn the plantation and attack the factory. Almost 2,000 hectares of the out-grower scheme were left without cultivation. Only the recipients of plots inside the Neshe irrigation scheme may use its water; others are refused. Across the three plants of the scheme, close to 240 MW, the study records that most households do not have access to the national grid.
cases.displaced_note: No count of households relocated for the Neshe dam is held here. The only figure is the field study's "approximately 1200", which the same sentence attributes to the people interviewed for the study and which follows the study's own words, "Exact figures are difficult to find". The study's other figure in that sentence, 3,115 households resettled, is for the earlier Fincha dam, is taken from another work, and belongs to a dam completed in 1973 with World Bank support, decades before this loan.
cases.outcome: The dam was completed on 17 November 2011 and inaugurated on 17 December 2011 (AidData record 92137). The study records the out-grower land dispute running to 2017 and almost 2,000 hectares left uncultivated.

cases.confidence_note: The unpaid compensation, the abandoned houses and the out-grower dispute all rest on one source: a peer-reviewed field study based on interviews with people in the area, published in 2019. AidData's own record reproduces that study's passage and cites it, so it is not a second source. No government, utility or lender document recording these harms was located, and the lender has published nothing on the project's social effects. The study's quotations about land taken without compensation at the Fincha and Amerti reservoirs belong to the two earlier stages of the scheme, built before this loan - Fincha completed in 1973 with World Bank support, Amerti in 1987 financed by the European Economic Community - and are not relied on here. The study gives the dam's completion two ways: its results section says Neshe Dam was completed in 2011, and its study-area section says the reservoir on the Neshe River was built in 2012. The study and AidData give the cost two ways: US$137 million of construction costs in the study, a $147.3 million contract and about $125.205 million of loan in AidData. The study puts the plant at 95 MW and 38 m high; AidData calls it 97 MW.
cx: China Eximbank subsidiary loans for the Neshe dam
cases.whole: The dam was built to generate power and to irrigate about 6,000 hectares of sugar cane for the state-owned Fincha Sugar Factory, and the plantation it feeds grew from 6,000 to almost 20,000 hectares. Since 1991 Ethiopia's power output rose from 400 MW to over 4,000 MW and national sugar production from 150,000 tons a year to well over 300,000 tons a year (Land 8(9):135). AidData records that this was reportedly the first EPC project a Chinese company undertook in East Africa.

cases.title: Cheddi Jagan airport expansion: engineer buried in a pit collapse
cases.point: Centroid of Cheddi Jagan International Airport (OpenStreetMap relation 11166939). The soil-testing spot where the two men were buried was more than a mile from the base where other workers were, according to a worker who spoke to Stabroek News.

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: Government concessional loan of RMB 825,000,000 [CHINA EXIMBANK GCL No. (2012) 32 Total No. (434) No. 1420203052012112030] signed with the Government of Guyana on 2 November 2012: 2% interest, a 5-year grace period, a 20-year maturity, a management fee of 0.75% (RMB 6,187,500) and a commitment fee of 0.5%. The proceeds were to cover 94.2% of a $138,000,000 contract between Guyana's Ministry of Public Works and Communications and China Harbour Engineering Company Ltd signed on 11 November 2011. As of 31 December 2020 the loan's total amount outstanding, including principal and capitalised interest, was RMB 673,698,000 (AidData record 36574). No World Bank P-number exists for this financing.

cases.conditions: The loan financed a commercial contract with a Chinese contractor, China Harbour Engineering Company, awarded ten days before Guyana's November 2011 national and regional elections (AidData record 36574).

companies.name: China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC) Ltd
companies.role: EPC contractor for the airport expansion and the employer of the two engineers
companies.desc: Chinese contractor for ports, dredging, land reclamation, roads and railways, set up in 1980 and a subsidiary of China Communications Construction Company (CCCC).

cases.community: On Thursday 17 September 2015 two CHEC engineers were buried when a humus pit caved in at the Timehri site. Police said that at about 12:35 pm a Chinese national of 23, whose name Demerara Waves gives as Lui Li, was doing soil testing and was trapped beneath a quantity of soil that caved in on him, and that he was pronounced dead on arrival at the Diamond Diagnostic Centre (Demerara Waves, 17 September 2015). Stabroek News, which spells the name Liu Li, reported that he was pronounced dead at the Georgetown Public Hospital and that his colleague Zhang Yixun was an admitted patient there, and quoted a press release from the Ministry of Public Infrastructure saying the humus pit collapsed at about 10.40 am and trapped the two men; the release said CHEC is responsible for the health and safety of its employees at the work site. A worker at the site said Li had been buried about 20 minutes before he could be dug out and that Zhang, who had tried to rescue him, was submerged up to his neck (Stabroek News, 18 September 2015). A preliminary report by the Labour, Occupational Safety and Health Department of Guyana's Ministry of Social Protection, reported on 5 October 2015, found that the accident was not reported to the ministry; that both men had begun working in Guyana on 6 September that year, had no prior work experience and had graduated from universities in China in July; that the sub-lot was "submerged with underground water"; that "the soil texture at the sub-lot was loose, waterlogged, and it was the least unstable type of soil"; that Li was in a bending position while inserting the vane shear apparatus into the ground when he was covered by slush, and that the injured man was covered up to his waist at the same time; that a site engineer told the team the area had been excavated in a slope but the team saw no slope; and that the accident scene, though cordoned off, had been tampered with. The report also found that CHEC's contract had workers on ten hours a day, seven days a week, that wage records for local workers showed no overtime paid, and that the wage records for Chinese employees did not carry the names of the dead or the injured man. The company said it had committed to compensating the dead man's family and had met them in China about burial arrangements, but the report said no proof of such financial assistance was seen. Li was cremated in Guyana and his ashes taken to China. The Diamond Diagnostic Centre was unable to treat him, and with no ambulance available a CHEC vehicle took him to the Georgetown Public Hospital Corporation, where Chinese doctors treated him; the injured man was treated at the Diamond facility (Guyana Chronicle, 5 October 2015).
cases.killed_note: Liu Li, an engineer employed by the contractor, died when the pit he was testing caved in. His colleague Zhang Yixun was hospitalised.
cases.outcome: The public infrastructure minister, David Patterson, asked for an immediate investigation into the incident, and a team of investigators including the Environmental Protection Agency was to visit the site the next day (Stabroek News, 18 September 2015). The ministry gave CHEC a list of measures to put in place, including keeping correct wage records for every employee, training workers regularly on safety and health, posting the occupational safety and health Act at the worksite, reporting accidents in time as the law requires, registering with the labour department and compensating the injured employee. The ministry asked for passports, work permits, signed employment contracts in Chinese and English, wage records, an autopsy report, National Insurance Scheme records and tax records; the company had not provided the work permits, the contracts, the wage records, the autopsy report, the insurance records or the tax records by the time the report was reported on. The report set out three grounds on which legal action could be taken against CHEC: failing to apply for registration of an industrial establishment under section 7(1) of the Occupational Safety and Health Act, chapter 99:10; failing to report the accident within the time the Act's section 69(1) stipulates; and failing to produce wages records under section 10 of the Labour Act, chapter 98:01. On 29 September the minister within the Ministry of Social Protection, Simona Broomes, allowed CHEC to restart work on the airport expansion while warning its representatives to comply with Guyana's laws, and said the death of Li and the injury of Yixun were the result of negligence (Guyana Chronicle, 5 October 2015). The expansion was still unfinished in 2022, ten years after it began, with the contract having expired on 31 December 2018 and costs rising from $138 million to more than $160 million (AidData record 36574).

The report itself is not published. The sources differ on three points, all printed above: the ministry put the time of the collapse at about 10.40 am and the police at about 12.35 pm; Demerara Waves has him pronounced dead on arrival at the Diamond Diagnostic Centre and Stabroek News at the Georgetown Public Hospital, while the labour report says Diamond could not treat him and he was taken on to the Georgetown hospital; and a worker told Stabroek News the injured man was submerged up to his neck, while the labour report says he was covered up to his waist. Whether the family was paid is not established: the company said it had committed to compensate them, and the report says no proof was seen.
cx: China Eximbank concessional loan for the Cheddi Jagan airport expansion
cases.whole: The loan paid for a 3.3 km runway extension to take Boeing 747-400 aircraft, a new terminal, boarding bridges, lifts, escalators, a departure control system and about 300 cameras. Guyana's auditor general opened a value-for-money audit in 2019; a former auditor general, Anand Goolsarran, said in April 2022 that the project had failed completely to deliver its objectives, outputs, outcomes and impacts, and in September 2020 noted that President Irfaan Ali had identified 71 defects to be rectified. The public works minister said in December 2021 that the total cost would not exceed $200 million (AidData record 36574).

cases.title: Booby Alley clearance: an eviction writ, a rubber bullet and an arrest
cases.place: Booby Alley, Point, St John's, Antigua and Barbuda
cases.point: Booby Lane in the Point area of St John's (OpenStreetMap way 1081942197, tagged urban residential).

lenders.name: Government of China
lenders.role: EC$100 million grant agreement signed in October 2018 with the Government of Antigua and Barbuda for the Affordable Housing Project (AidData record 89551), with a further RMB 80 million committed under an Economic and Technical Cooperation Agreement signed on 26 November 2019 (AidData records 92146, 92147 and 92148). The site was to be turned over to Chinese contractors to build condominium-style homes (Pointe Xpress, 5 April 2023). The agreement to build 150 two-bedroom units is dated August 2021 by the Antigua Observer and 18 August 2022 by Antigua News. No World Bank P-number exists for this financing.

cases.conditions: The housing is being built under a turn-key agreement between the two governments, with Chinese contractors doing the work (Antigua News, 12 October 2023; Pointe Xpress, 5 April 2023).

companies.name: Ministry of Housing, Lands and Urban Renewal, Antigua and Barbuda
companies.role: Government ministry that arranged the temporary housing and the acquisition of the Booby Alley land
companies.desc: The ministry responsible for state lands and housing in Antigua and Barbuda. It built temporary housing complexes on Crown land at Bay Street and Reginald Stevens Street to hold Booby Alley residents while the site was cleared, and a Booby Alley Project Mobilisation Office, with its own mobilisation manager, handled the moves. The sources name no construction company.

cases.community: Booby Alley is a low-income area of less than two acres in the Point district of St John's, built up with small chattel houses. The plan was to clear it, move the residents to temporary homes at Bay Street and Reginald Stevens Street, and rebuild it with condominium-style units. The housing minister, Maria Browne, said in July 2019 that the residents would be relocated to Bay Street temporarily (Antigua Observer, 1 July 2019). AidData records that 12 families from Booby Alley received keys to temporary three-bedroom houses at a handover in March 2021 and that one family, supported by some other residents, staged a protest and refused to move for months. In April 2023 the project's mobilisation manager, Kem Hodge, said more than two hundred and forty persons had been relocated, free of charge, which he described as the vast majority of residents, and that the area had to be cleared by the end of that month and handed to the Chinese contractors. He said a five-bedroom concrete house had been secured as a temporary home for the remaining family of nine, the O'Mardes, that an agreement had been reached on the advice of their lawyers, Leon Chaku Symister and Sherfield Bowen, and that the government had sought and received a court order for their removal (Pointe Xpress, 5 April 2023). Antigua News reported that the head of the family had signed a consent order on 21 March 2023, under which a five-bedroom, two-bathroom property would be built for them to live in until the housing development was completed, the family would pay the utilities and maintenance of that home, and the properties were to be vacated within 24 hours of the alternative accommodation being ready and no later than 28 March. On Tuesday 4 April 2023, at about 12:30 pm, police from St John's police station went with a bailiff of the High Court of Justice to enforce a writ. Police said Joel O'Marde refused to comply, hurled threats at the police and the court officer, armed himself with a weapon, and that officers used non-lethal measures to subdue him and take him into custody (police statement, 5 April 2023). An assistant commissioner of police, Clifton Cabral, said the bailiff read the writ, the family agreed to it and began packing, and that one son kept threatening police, said he had a loaded gun, armed himself with a knife and barricaded himself inside; police called for backup, broke the door and used rubber bullets to control him. Cabral put the episode at at least three hours; a later Antigua News report calls it a four-hour incident. O'Marde was taken to a medical centre, where a doctor treated him for bruises, and then handed back into police custody (Antigua News, 6 April 2023). He was charged with disorderly conduct, threatening language and being armed with an offensive weapon, told the court on 6 April 2023 that he was not ready to plead, and was granted bail of $2,000 with a $300 cash component, with reporting to the St John's police station every Monday and Saturday; the magistrate, Dane Hamilton Jr, adjourned the matter to 5 June (Antigua News, 7 April 2023). Hodge said a High Court judge had fined O'Marde $1,000 for contempt of court. By 12 October 2023 a trailer had towed away the final houses and the land was clear; only three houses had remained before that. In late September 2023 the compulsory acquisition of one plot of less than 0.05 acres was avoided when its occupants, the siblings Dawn and Desiree Browne, reached agreement with the government (Antigua News, 12 October 2023).
cases.displaced_note: No count of people relocated is held here. The figure in the sources is "more than two hundred and forty persons", a floor, and it is the project's own mobilisation manager's, given to the government-owned Pointe Xpress on 5 April 2023. AidData's record separately says 12 families received keys to temporary homes at a handover in March 2021; that figure was found only in AidData's record. Antigua News reports that after consultation many families vacated the area and were relocated, without a number.
cases.suppression: Police accompanying a High Court bailiff shot Joel O'Marde with a rubber bullet on 4 April 2023 and took him into custody; police said they used non-lethal measures after he threatened officers and the court officer and armed himself with a weapon. A doctor treated him for bruises. He was charged with disorderly conduct, threatening language and being armed with an offensive weapon, was granted bail, and the matter was adjourned to 5 June 2023. The project's mobilisation manager said a High Court judge fined him $1,000 for contempt of court. The opposition leader, Harold Lovell, said the problem was approached in the wrong way from the very beginning and that it should never have been a confrontational issue, that the government should have assured residents of a right to return, that "we are not absolutely clear what the terms of the Chinese grant or loan is", and that if the funds were for the benefit of the residents of Booby Alley they ought to benefit as intended (Antigua Observer, 14 December 2022). Shortly before that report the Prime Minister, Gaston Browne, had threatened the residents remaining in the area with a court order to vacate.
cases.outcome: The site was cleared by October 2023 and 150 two-bedroom units are to be built there. Construction had not begun a year after the agreement was signed, and the government said it was worried that the Chinese government might withdraw its support because of how long it was taking to persuade some residents to accept temporary housing elsewhere (Antigua News, 12 October 2023). Prime Minister Gaston Browne said most of the units would be heavily subsidised rentals and that those who had homes in the Booby Alley area would be able to own a home at a substantially reduced cost and would be given credit for their existing home, whatever its condition (AidData record 89551).

cases.confidence_note: The eviction, the rubber bullet, the arrest, the charges, the bail terms and the bruises are carried by a police statement and by Antigua News, and the consent order of 21 March 2023 and its terms are reported by Antigua News, not only by the project. The relocation count of more than 240 persons and the court fine for contempt rest on one statement by the project's mobilisation manager, carried by the government-owned Pointe Xpress; the count is also a floor. No court record of the writ, the consent order, the contempt fine or the charges was located: a web search of the Antigua and Barbuda High Court material indexed online returned nothing on this matter, and the Antigua News, Pointe Xpress and Antigua Observer reports listed here were read in full. The 12 families at the March 2021 handover come only from AidData's record. The date of the agreement for 150 units differs between sources: August 2021 (Antigua Observer, 14 December 2022) and 18 August 2022 (Antigua News, 12 October 2023). What the residents were paid, if anything, for their chattel houses is not recorded in these sources.
cx: Chinese grant for the Booby Alley Affordable Housing Project
cases.whole: The grant was to pay for 250 homes in all: 150 at Booby Alley, 50 at Bolans and 50 on Barbuda. Temporary houses handed over in March 2021 were three-bedroom, about 1,200 square feet, with a laundry room, bathroom, kitchen and living room, and electricity, water and internet connections (AidData record 89551). The government calls the Booby Alley scheme social housing giving occupants a route to home ownership (Antigua News, 12 October 2023).

lenders_add.name: China Eximbank: the two signed loan agreements, 2014 and 2015
lenders_add.role: The same lender as above, with the agreements themselves. Two agreements with the Government of Uganda worth $1,435,158,682 together for the 600 MW dam and its transmission lines, ratified by Uganda's Parliament on 27 February 2015: a preferential buyer's credit of $789,337,275.36 signed on 18 December 2014 at 2% interest with a 20-year maturity and a 7-year grace period (AidData record 30919), and a buyer's credit of $645,821,407.12 signed on 20 February 2015 at LIBOR plus a 3.5% margin with a 15-year maturity and a 5-year grace period (AidData record 36211); the 3.827% all-in rate is AidData's own calculation from the November 2014 average six-month LIBOR. Between them they were to finance 85% of a $1,688,421,979.39 contract between Uganda's Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development and Sinohydro Corporation Limited signed on 16 August 2013. Uganda's Aid Management Platform records the preferential credit 85.4% disbursed, $674,527,385.55 in 24 disbursements between 2015 and 2020, and the buyer's credit 97% disbursed, $625,602,535.38 in 31 disbursements between 2015 and 2022; the finance ministry's public debt report for 2021/22 instead puts disbursements under the buyer's credit at $581,678,517 as of 31 December 2021, with $517,096,376.38 outstanding. No World Bank P-number exists for this financing.

sources_add.title: Workers dying at Chinese sites rise
Three feared dead after accident at Karuma dam
AidData Global Chinese Development Finance Dataset, record 30919: China Eximbank preferential buyer's credit for the 600 MW Karuma Hydropower Dam and associated transmission lines

fields_add.community: Workers on the site were hurt and killed. The Independent reported on 12 December 2016, from letters between the contractor Sinohydro and the government's project supervisor Energy Infratech and from accounts by workers and insiders, that Rogers Twine's body was smashed on 23 September: at about 05:45 he was working inside the tunnels when a blasting happened and he was hit by flying stones and debris. Sources knowledgeable about the incident said a Chinese blasting supervisor had apparently ordered the blasting without alerting Twine as standard operating procedures required. Energy Infratech raised the Twine case with Sinohydro, noting that the blasting standards and operating procedure were not followed and the blaster was not competent. Its project manager, R.RS Manian, wrote: "We fail to understand as to how such a serious lapse can happen if proper procedures are followed", and the contractor was directed to stop all works involving blasting activities throughout the project site. In a letter of 6 October Manian wrote that blasting procedure had not been followed by the blaster in charge, that some blasters' permits to use blasting materials had expired while others had no permit from the Internal Affairs Ministry, and directed that the blaster in charge be suspended until an accident investigation committee reported and that all blasters without permits be suspended indefinitely. In a presentation seen by The Independent, officials of the Uganda Electricity Generation Company told energy ministry officials that eight people had died at the dam site before June of that year. A health and safety expert with knowledge of Karuma, speaking off the record, said that in some instances over 30 cases of serious accidents had been recorded at the dam in a month. When officials visited Gulu Independent Hospital on 9 September they found three such cases: Aguma Safri, Ocaya Gensis and Isabirye Safiq, injured during tunnel excavation and taken to hospital without their cases being recorded. Another worker fell off a project truck, lost almost all his teeth and was taken from the hospital to an unknown place before investigators arrived. Energy Infratech wrote to Sinohydro: "We have also identified gaps in your incident and accident reporting procedures, characterised by coached reporting of witnesses, and concealing of information resulting to non-reporting", and "we find you violating the Occupational Health and Safety Act." At the beginning of October the site, with over 5,000 workers, had no experienced doctor at its clinic apart from a Chinese doctor who worked as an administrator and did not treat Ugandans. The head of the generation company, Harrison Mutikanga, said in November that the deaths already recorded at Karuma were unusually higher than those recorded in similar projects, but was also optimistic: "But we are engaging the contractor. The new leadership is serious about getting the contractor to have all these problems solved." Sinohydro's executive president for East and Southern Africa, Wang Yantao, visiting the site in November, promised that conditions would improve.
fields_add.killed_note: Rogers Twine was hit by flying stones and debris from a blast inside the tunnels on 23 September and The Independent describes his body as smashed, in a report of 12 December 2016 that does not state that he died; it is not counted. The cause given for the blast being fired without alerting him is attributed in that report to sources knowledgeable about the incident and is hedged as apparent; the project supervisor's own letters say instead that blasting standards and procedure were not followed and the blaster was not competent. Officials of the Uganda Electricity Generation Company told energy ministry officials in a presentation that eight people had died at the dam site before June of that year; no cause is given for any of them, so none is counted. Yuding Yong, the manager of the site's water treatment plant, was found hanging with an electric cable around his neck after managers detained him at his residence when a machine operator reported that he had polluted the water; The Independent reports it as a suicide, Sinohydro published no official report, and several accounts of the cause circulated, one of them from the deputy project manager that Yuding had planned to disrupt the project and one from Wang Yantao that he was frustrated at being about to lose his job. In August 2018 a truck carrying workers failed to brake and hit a side wall at the dam; The East African reported at least three dead, while the dam's management said several workers were injured and no fatalities were recorded (Nile Post, 31 August 2018). None of these are counted.
fields_add.confidence_note: The worker deaths and injuries rest on The Independent's December 2016 investigation, which quotes letters between Sinohydro and the government's project supervisor that are not published, and attributes several of its accounts to unnamed workers, insiders and an off-the-record expert. Sinohydro's regional head said conditions would improve and the generation company's head said it was engaging the contractor. The death toll in the August 2018 truck crash is disputed between The East African and the dam's management.

sources_add.title: AidData Global Chinese Development Finance Dataset, record 98775: ICBC share of the $5.988 billion syndicated loan for the Las Bambas Copper Project

fields_add.conditions: AidData's description of the 2014 project facility agreement with Minera Las Bambas S.A.C. gives the syndicate's shares one bank at a time, as approximations: China Development Bank is the leading bank and responsible for about 50% of the $5.988 billion loan (AidData record 55426), the co-leading bank, the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, for about 30% (record 98775), and Bank of China (Sydney Branch) and the Export-Import Bank of China for about 10% each (records 98776 and 98774). AidData's per-bank dollar figures are those percentages applied to the facility, so they are not separate evidence of the shares. The facility ran at six-month LIBOR plus a margin AidData records as not exceeding 365 basis points, with an 18-year maturity, and $4.119 billion of it had been drawn down as of 2014. ICBC also provided a letter of guarantee for the operation of the project. Approximately $469.0 million of these borrowings, against $699.0 million in 2018, is guaranteed on a several basis by China Minmetals Non-ferrous Metals Holding, China Minmetals Corporation, Guoxin International Investment and CITIC Corporation in proportion to their shareholdings in the Las Bambas joint venture group. The owner of the mine, Minera Las Bambas S.A.C., is a joint venture of MMG with 62.5%, GUOXIN International Investment Group with 22.5% and CITIC Metal with 15%; AidData notes that MMG is a wholly owned subsidiary of Guoxin International Investment. A separate $969 million acquisition facility is recorded under AidData records 55427, 98780, 98781 and 98783.
fields_add.confidence_note: The $5.988 billion is the facility, not any one bank's loan. The per-bank shares are AidData's own prose, given as "about" figures, and AidData names no document for them.
